notes: The charge concerns the scribes’ handling of the LORD’s instruction. The Hebrew does not explain here precisely how their pen has made it false.
“My daughter, my people” keeps the poem’s picture of the people as a wounded daughter. Voices move between the people, the lamenting speaker, and God; not every transition is explicitly identified.

Verse 13’s gathering/removal verb and final clause are difficult. “Sweep them away” is one reading; the ending may also concern things given to them that overtake them. The rare opening expression in verse 18 is also uncertain; the rendering connects it with failing comfort in sorrow.
This edition preserves the existing Hebrew numbering: 8:23 is 9:1 in many English Bibles, and the following chapter has twenty-five verses.
vocabulary: God’s ruling or ordered way; the contrast is with birds that recognize their seasons.
An aromatic substance used for healing. Gilead was associated with this product.

notes: The Hebrew phrase about a brother’s scheming echoes the verb associated with Jacob’s name and his supplanting of Esau.
The arrow’s description is uncertain. The written form suggests slaughtering; the recorded reading may suggest a sharpened or deadly arrow.
The last line can concern homes being torn down or people being driven out of them.
The paradox of being circumcised yet uncircumcised is retained. The passage ends by distinguishing bodily circumcision from the condition of the heart.
vocabulary: A bitter plant, here paired with poisoned water as an image of judgment.
Women skilled in leading communal lament.
Hebrew hesed: enduring loyalty and kindness in relationship, here alongside justice and righteousness.

notes: “Scarecrows in a cucumber field” is one reading of the compressed Hebrew; a rigid palm-like object has also been proposed. Verse 8 likewise compresses its scorn into the assertion that the idols’ instruction is wood.
The pinned Hebrew names Uphaz. Its location is uncertain; this edition does not replace it with Ophir.
This verse is in Aramaic, surrounded by Hebrew. Its verbs for making and perishing sound alike.
The final Hebrew clause is literally “so that they find.” Its object is unstated; “feel it” relates the finding to the distress just announced.
vocabulary: An allotted share. Here the LORD is Jacob’s portion, while Israel is called God’s inheritance.
An image for leaders responsible for the people, pictured as their flock.

sections.1: Made gods and the living God

notes: This verse is unusually difficult. “The many” may name those doing wrong. The relation of “sacred meat” to “pass away from you” is uncertain; proposed readings often change the vowels or consonants. The draft retains the difficult wording without claiming that its syntax is settled.
“Fruit” in verse 19 renders the tree’s “food” or “bread.” In verse 20, “innermost being” renders “kidneys,” paired with the heart as the inner seat of feeling and intent.
vocabulary: A fierce furnace image for the experience of slavery in Egypt.
A contemptuous designation for Baal in this accusation.

notes: The “he” in verse 4 is not explicitly identified; it may refer to God or the prophet. The Jordan’s “pride” in verse 5 can describe its luxuriant thickets or swelling waters.
The unusual expression is rendered “speckled bird of prey.” A hyena-like beast has also been proposed; the surrounding line speaks of birds of prey.
The promise of return includes the neighboring peoples named in verse 14. Their place among God’s people is then described conditionally.
vocabulary: The language is that of a dispute brought for judgment; the prophet asks God about justice.
The people and land belonging to God; the term recurs through this lament.

notes: Perath is the Hebrew name commonly used for the Euphrates. A local site near Jeremiah’s home has also been proposed for this sign-act. The place-name is retained without settling the question.

Verse 20’s written form addresses a feminine singular figure; the recorded reading begins with plural commands. Verse 21’s appointment/friendship clause is difficult. Verse 22 literally says the “heels” are violated; with the exposed skirts, it evokes bodily and sexual humiliation.
Cush lay south of Egypt. The comparison concerns the inability to change an established condition; it does not call the Cushite’s skin evil.
Jerusalem is addressed as a woman. The accusation and violent exposure belong to the passage’s own imagery and are retained as such.
vocabulary: A linen garment worn around the waist, used here in a symbolic action.
The king’s mother, who could hold a recognized position at court.

notes: The gates and ground are personified as sharing Judah’s distress. The word rendered “cracked” can also describe being shattered or dismayed.
The prayer compares God’s apparent absence to a temporary resident and God’s apparent inability to help to a stunned man. These are the lament’s questions, not a narrator’s explanation.
The lamenting voice is not fully identified. The last line of verse 18 may describe going into an unfamiliar land or moving about without understanding what is happening.
vocabulary: Reservoirs that store water, often rainwater.
An image associated with God’s sanctuary and rule.

sections.1: Drought and a plea for help
sections.10: Promises the LORD did not send

notes: Several phrases in this section are difficult. Verse 8’s “anguish” renders an obscure term. Verse 11 follows the recorded reading as a promise of release; strengthening is another interpretation. Verse 14 retains the pinned verb “make pass,” with “you” supplied. “Make you serve,” found in some translations, follows a different reading, also present in 17:4.
Verse 16 moves from “words” to the recorded singular “word.” In verse 18, the prophet compares God to a stream whose water cannot be relied on.
vocabulary: To toss grain so the wind separates it from chaff; here an image of scattering and loss.
The Hebrew repeats the same root in returning, restoring, and the direction others should take.

notes: The prohibitions on marriage, mourning, and feasting are directed to Jeremiah in this setting, as signs of the announced disaster.
Bread is implied in the mourning practice of verse 7. Verse 18 calls the detestable objects “corpses,” keeping the contemptuous image rather than treating it as a description of living gods.
vocabulary: A drink offered to comfort mourners.
An oath formula, here retold around a future return from exile.

sections.1: A life set apart as a sign

notes: The engraving point is made of a very hard material, traditionally “diamond”; “hard stone” avoids a precise mineral claim. Verse 2’s relationship to the surrounding lines is uncertain: it may concern children remembering the altars or attachment to altars compared with attachment to children. Verse 3 preserves the abrupt address to “my mountain.”
The recorded reading says the tree does not “see” the heat, rendered “notice.” The written form can be read “fear,” as many translations do.
“Innermost being” renders “kidneys.” The partridge saying uses an ancient image of brooding over another’s eggs to portray unjustly acquired wealth; it is not a modern zoological description.

Verse 13 retains the source’s shift from “you” to “me.” Verse 16’s “shepherding in your service” renders a difficult phrase, literally “being a shepherd after you”; another proposed reading concerns not urging God to bring disaster.
vocabulary: A dry region; here the image emphasizes a barren, salty place.
The low foothills west of Judah’s hill country.

sections.19: At the gates on the Sabbath

notes: The vessel here is still workable clay. The explanation explicitly describes God relenting from announced disaster or good in response to a nation’s conduct.

The Hebrew expressions for the rocky setting and the waters are uncertain. The draft retains Lebanon’s snow and cold flowing water without changing “foreign” or distant waters into an unmarked mountain-source reading.
These are the prophet’s petitions against his opponents. Their violence and the request that guilt not be forgiven remain explicit; the text does not turn them into a general instruction to readers.
vocabulary: Literally “the two stones,” the potter’s working apparatus.
A harsh drying wind, used here as an image of scattering.

notes: The Potsherd Gate’s precise location is uncertain. “Empty out” in verse 7 echoes the sound of the Hebrew word for the jar.
The siege’s cannibalism is stated directly. Unlike the workable clay of chapter 18, the broken vessel here cannot be repaired. Burial at Topheth follows the lack of space elsewhere.
vocabulary: Fired clay pottery, brittle enough to shatter.
The heavenly bodies worshiped on the rooftops in this accusation.

sections.14: The warning in the temple court

notes: “Terror on Every Side” translates Magor-missabib. The verb rendered “deceived” can also mean enticed or persuaded; the forceful protest is retained. “Deceived” and “prevail” recur in the opponents’ words, followed by the LORD’s prevailing protection.
Praise gives way immediately to a curse on the day of birth. The draft preserves this sequence and the final unanswered lament.
vocabulary: A device for restraining a prisoner’s body; its exact construction here is uncertain.
Literally “kidneys,” paired with the heart as in 11:20 and 17:10.
